title: Consonant Gradation Basics
subtitle: Alternation between strong and weak consonant stems in words
keyPoint: Estonian words alternate between strong and weak grades, typically weakening consonants like k, p, and t when suffixes are added.

mistakes.note: The noun 'pank' undergoes gradation (kk -> g/ng) in the genitive case to form 'panga'.
The verb 'lugema' has the weak stem 'loe-' in the first person present tense.
The word 'tuba' drops the 'b' in the weak grade, yielding the stem 'toa-'.

quiz.question: Complete the genitive form: 'See on minu uue ___ (kodu) aadress.'
quiz.explanation: 'Kodu' retains 'kodu' in the genitive singular (shortening/weak stem).

quiz.question: Choose the correct genitive of 'pank':
quiz.explanation: The strong cluster 'nk' weakens to 'ng', giving 'panga'.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank with the correct verb form: 'Ma ___ (lugema) seda lehte.'
quiz.explanation: The first-person singular 'ma' requires the weak-stem form 'loen'.

quiz.question: Identify the weak-grade form of 'tuba':
quiz.explanation: 'Tuba' weakens by losing 'b', leaving the stem 'toa-'.

tip: Memorize the first three basic forms of every noun together to master gradation effortlessly.

title: The Three Base Forms of Nouns
subtitle: Nominative, Genitive, and Partitive as the building blocks for all cases
keyPoint: All 14 Estonian noun cases are formed by attaching endings to either the Genitive stem (singular cases) or the Partitive stem.

mistakes.note: Numbers greater than one require the noun in the Partitive singular.
Postpositions like 'peal' require the preceding noun to be in the Genitive case.
Objects of partial or indefinite desire/consumption must be in the Partitive case.

quiz.question: Which case is used directly after numbers higher than one (e.g., 'viis ___')?
quiz.explanation: Numerals (except one) govern the Partitive singular.

quiz.question: What is the Genitive singular of 'laud' (table)?
quiz.explanation: 'Laud' weakens by dropping 'd', resulting in 'laua'.

quiz.question: Identify the Nominative form in: 'kass', 'kassi', 'kasse', 'kassiga'.
quiz.explanation: 'Kass' is the basic dictionary/Nominative form.

quiz.question: Complete the phrase: 'Ma loen huvitavat ___ (leht)'.
quiz.explanation: The direct object of ongoing reading is Partitive: 'lehte'.

tip: Always learn vocabulary in triplets: 'raamat, raamatu, raamatut'.

title: Internal Local Cases
subtitle: Moving into, staying inside, and moving out of enclosed spaces
keyPoint: Internal local cases add -sse (Illative: into), -s (Inessive: inside), and -st (Elative: out of) to the singular Genitive stem.

useCases.label: Exiting an Interior
useCases.example: Ta tuleb hilja töölt koju ja astub autost välja.

mistakes.note: Expressing location inside a city requires the Inessive suffix -s on the Genitive stem.
'Lähen' requires motion into (Illative), not stationary Inessive (-s).
Expressing movement from a place requires the Elative ending -st.

quiz.question: Which sentence means 'I live in a room'?
quiz.explanation: Inessive case ending '-s' denotes staying inside: 'toas'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form for 'out of the forest': 'Tuleme ___ (mets).'
quiz.explanation: Movement out of an interior uses the Elative suffix '-st' -> 'metsast'.

quiz.question: Complete the direction: 'Ta läheb uude ___ (korter).'
quiz.explanation: Movement into a place takes the Illative '-sse' -> 'korterisse'.

quiz.question: What question word corresponds to the Inessive case (-s)?
quiz.explanation: 'Kus?' (Where?) asks about location within a place.

tip: Attach -s, -st, and -sse directly to the Genitive stem (e.g., korteri -> korteris, korterist, korterisse).

title: External Local Cases
subtitle: Moving onto surfaces, staying on or at locations, and leaving them
keyPoint: External local cases attach -le (Allative: onto), -l (Adessive: on/at), and -lt (Ablative: off of) to the Genitive stem, also expressing possession.

mistakes.note: Estonian has no verb 'to have'; use the person in Adessive (mul) + on + thing.
To say 'on the table', use the Adessive suffix -l on the genitive stem.
'Give to me' takes the short allative 'mulle' or full 'minule'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I have a dog' in Estonian?
quiz.explanation: The possessive structure is [Person in Adessive] + on + [Noun in Nominative]: 'Mul on koer.'

quiz.question: Choose the correct case for movement onto an open area: 'Lapsed lähevad ___ (õu).'
quiz.explanation: Direction onto/towards an open area uses the Allative suffix '-le'.

quiz.question: Which suffix marks the Ablative case (from a surface)?
quiz.explanation: The Ablative ending is '-lt' (e.g., laualt = from the table).

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Sõnastik seisab minu ___ (laud).'
quiz.explanation: Position on top of a table requires the Adessive case '-l': 'laual'.

tip: The Adessive case (-l) does double duty: spatial position ('on') and ownership ('mul on' = I have).

title: Present Tense Conjugation and Negation
subtitle: Conjugating personal endings and using the universal negative word 'ei'
keyPoint: Add personal endings (-n, -d, -b, -me, -te, -vad) to the present stem, and negate simply by placing 'ei' before the bare stem.

mistakes.note: Never keep personal endings in negative sentences; use 'ei' + bare present stem.
The negative stem 'ei ela' is invariant for all persons, singular and plural.
Third-person singular 'tema/ta' takes the personal ending '-b'.

quiz.question: How do you conjugate 'õppima' for 'meie' in the present tense?
quiz.explanation: The first-person plural ending is '-me': 'meie õpime'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct negative form: 'Nemad ___ siin.'
quiz.explanation: Negation uses invariant 'ei' plus the present stem without personal endings: 'ei tööta'.

quiz.question: Select the correct ending for 'sina':
quiz.explanation: Second-person singular 'sina/sa' takes the ending '-d'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Kas te ___ eesti keelt?' (rääkima)
quiz.explanation: 'Teie/te' matches the ending '-te': 'räägite'.

tip: To make any verb negative in the present tense, simply take the 'ma' form (e.g., 'elan'), drop the '-n' ('ela'), and add 'ei' in front: 'ei ela' for all persons!

title: Partitive Singular with Numbers and Quantifiers
subtitle: Use the Partitive Singular after numbers two and above as well as quantity words
keyPoint: All cardinal numbers from two upwards and indefinite quantifiers require the following countable noun to be in the Partitive Singular.

mistakes.note: Numbers take the Partitive singular, never the Nominative plural.
The number 'üks' (one) takes the Nominative singular, not Partitive.
While uncountable nouns take Partitive singular, countable nouns after 'palju' usually take Partitive plural.

quiz.question: I need two tickets: 'Mul on vaja kaks ___.'
quiz.explanation: Cardinal numerals from 2 upwards govern the Partitive singular form 'piletit'.

quiz.question: There is only one apple left: 'Laual on ainult üks ___.'
quiz.explanation: The number 'üks' is followed by the Nominative singular form 'õun'.

quiz.question: Do you want a cup of coffee: 'Kas sa soovid tassi ___?'
quiz.explanation: Indefinite substances and items following containers take the Partitive singular 'kohvi'.

quiz.question: We have three big rooms: 'Meil on kolm suurt ___.'
quiz.explanation: The Partitive singular of 'tuba' is 'tuba' (with short vowel and grade change), governed by 'kolm'.

tip: Always learn the first three base forms of every Estonian noun (Nominative, Genitive, Partitive); you cannot count without knowing the 3rd form!

title: The -ma vs. -da Infinitives
subtitle: Master when to use the supine (-ma) versus the standard infinitive (-da)
keyPoint: Use the -ma infinitive for motion, starting, and obligation (peama), and use the -da infinitive after modal verbs, preferences, and permissions.

cells: on hea, on raske, on tore

useCases.label: Desire and Ability (-da)
useCases.example: Kas sa oskad eesti keelt rääkida?

examples.en: Ma hakkan nüüd eesti keelt õppima.
Me läheme täna kinno uut filmi vaatama.

mistakes.note: 'Tahtma' (to want) must always govern the -da infinitive ('minna').
'Pidama' (must/have to) always requires the -ma infinitive.
Motion verbs indicating purpose (like 'minema') require the -ma form.

quiz.question: He has to work tomorrow: 'Ta peab homme ___.'
quiz.explanation: The modal verb 'pidama' strictly requires the -ma infinitive form ('töötama').

quiz.question: We want to sleep: 'Me tahame juba ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Tahtma' (to want) governs the -da infinitive ('magada').

quiz.question: Are you going outside to play: 'Kas sa lähed õue ___?'
quiz.explanation: Verbs of motion like 'minema' demand the -ma supine of purpose.

quiz.question: It is very pleasant to live here: 'Siin on väga meeldiv ___.'
quiz.explanation: Expressions of state or impersonal evaluations ('on meeldiv') take the -da infinitive.

tip: Remember the mnemonic: 'P-H-M' (Pean, Hakkan, Minema) all take -MA; almost all other common verbs like 'tahan' and 'saan' take -DA.

title: Simple Past Tense (Lihtminevik)
subtitle: Narrate completed past events using the -s and -sid past suffixes
keyPoint: The simple past adds -s for the 3rd person singular and regular endings (-n, -d, -me, -te, -sid) to the past stem, which often features -i- or consonant changes.

useCases.label: Chronological Narration
useCases.example: Ta ärkas, sõi ja läks tööle.

examples.en: Eile õhtul vaatasin ma huvitavat saadet.
Me tulime eile väga hilja koju.
Kas sa rääkisid sellest oma emale?

mistakes.note: The 3rd person singular past ending is -s, not -sin (which is 1st person).
'Lugen' is present tense; simple past requires the past stem with -sin ('lugesin').
Do not combine the verb 'olema' with simple past endings when narrating single past events.

quiz.question: Yesterday she wrote an email: 'Eile ___ ta pika e-kirja.'
quiz.explanation: The 3rd person singular past form of 'kirjutama' is 'kirjutas'.

quiz.question: Where did you (plural) travel last summer: 'Kuhu te eelmisel suvel ___?'
quiz.explanation: The 2nd person plural ending in lihtminevik is -site, giving 'reisisite'.

quiz.question: I saw that movie last week: 'Ma ___ seda filmi eelmisel nädalal.'
quiz.explanation: The 1st person singular simple past of 'nägema' is irregular: 'nägin'.

quiz.question: They were at home all evening: 'Nemad ___ terve õhtu kodus.'
quiz.explanation: The 3rd person plural past of 'olema' is 'olid'.

tip: Many common verbs show a vowel shift to '-i-' in the past stem: 'tegema' becomes 'tegi-', 'nägema' becomes 'nägi-', and 'tulema' becomes 'tuli-'.

title: Direct Object: Partitive vs. Total (Täissihitis vs. Osasihitis)
subtitle: Distinguish partial, ongoing, or negative actions from completed whole results
keyPoint: Use the Partitive object for negative, ongoing, or incomplete actions, but the Genitive/Nominative total object when a definite action is fully completed.

cells: He is reading a book (in progress).

useCases.label: Negative Sentences (Strict)
useCases.example: Ma ei söönud seda õuna ära.

mistakes.note: Any direct object in a negated sentence MUST be in the Partitive case.

mistakes.right: Ma söön õuna ära (or: sõin õuna ära).
mistakes.note: With resultative particle 'ära' expressing full completion, singular total object takes Genitive: 'sõin õuna ära' (here Genitive and Partitive of 'õun' differ: Partitive is 'õuna', Genitive is 'õuna'; for distinctive nouns: 'sõin kooki' vs 'sõin koogi ära').
In affirmative imperative commands targeting the whole item, use the Nominative total object.

quiz.question: I did not find the key: 'Ma ei leidnud ___ üles.'
quiz.explanation: Negative clauses universally demand the Partitive case object ('võtit').

quiz.question: He drank the cup of tea completely: 'Ta jõi tee ___ ära.'
quiz.explanation: Completed result action on a countable noun uses Genitive singular total object ('tassi').

quiz.question: Open the door! (Imperative command): 'Ava ___!'
quiz.explanation: Total objects in direct imperative commands appear in the Nominative case ('uks').

quiz.question: The boy is currently writing an essay: 'Poiss kirjutab praegu ___.'
quiz.explanation: Ongoing, uncompleted actions take a Partitive object ('kirjandit').

tip: Check for negation first! If the sentence has 'ei', the direct object is automatically Partitive 100% of the time.

title: Postpositions and Genitive Governance
subtitle: Express location, direction, and relations by placing adverbs after Genitive nouns
keyPoint: Most spatial and relational markers in Estonian are postpositions that follow a noun inflected in the Genitive case.

examples.en: Väike laps peitis end voodi alla.

mistakes.note: Estonian primarily uses postpositions (after the noun), and the noun must be in the Genitive case.
The noun preceding the postposition must be in Genitive ('laua'), not Nominative ('laud').
Sitting down is directional motion towards a surface, requiring the directional form '-le' ('peale'), not static 'peal'.

quiz.question: The cat is sleeping under the bed: 'Kass magab ___ all.'
quiz.explanation: Postpositions govern the Genitive singular case ('voodi').

quiz.question: Place the books onto the table: 'Pane raamatud laua ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Peale' indicates movement onto a surface (destination), answering 'kuhu?'.

quiz.question: The car stopped in front of the house: 'Auto peatus maja ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Ees' indicates stationary position in front of something, answering 'kus?'.

quiz.question: Our pharmacy is next to the shop: 'Apteek on poe ___.'
quiz.explanation: Static location beside something uses 'kõrval' ('kus?').

tip: Postpositions follow the same 3-way direction system as noun endings: -le/-te (whither? where to?), -l/-s (where?), and -lt/-st (whence? where from?).

title: Plural Formations (Nominative -d and Partitive Plural)
subtitle: Forming the plural subject with -d and master the multifaceted partitive plural endings
keyPoint: The nominative plural simply adds -d to the genitive singular stem, whereas the partitive plural takes endings like -sid, -id, or vowel changes depending on syllable structure.

examples.en: Need suured majad on väga vanad.
Mul on kodus kaks kassi ja kolm koera.

mistakes.note: Always attach the nominative plural marker -d to the genitive singular stem (raamatu), not the nominative singular.
Quantifying words like 'palju' (many/much) govern the partitive plural, not the nominative plural.
Existential negative clauses require the subject to be in the partitive plural (õunu), not nominative.

quiz.question: How do you form the nominative plural of 'maja' (genitive: 'maja')?
quiz.explanation: Add -d directly to the genitive singular stem 'maja' to make 'majad'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct partitive plural: 'Laual on palju ___ (kass - kassid).'
quiz.explanation: Short vowel-stem words like 'kass' take the vocalic or shortened partitive plural form 'kasse'.

quiz.question: Complete the negative sentence: 'Meil ei ole uusi ___ (arvuti).'
quiz.explanation: 'Arvuti' forms its partitive plural as 'arvuteid' (or 'arvutisid').

quiz.question: Which form represents the nominative plural for 'tüdruk' (genitive: 'tüdruku')?
quiz.explanation: Add -d to the genitive singular stem 'tüdruku' yielding 'tüdrukud'.

tip: Always memorize the first three base forms of every Estonian noun: Nominative, Genitive, and Partitive. The Genitive singular is your golden key to building the Nominative plural (-d).

title: Impersonal Voice in the Present (Umbisikuline Tegumood)
subtitle: Describing actions without mentioning a specific doer using -takse and -dakse
keyPoint: The impersonal present uses -takse or -dakse attached to the verb stem to express actions done by people in general, corresponding to 'one does', 'people do', or passive voice in English.

mistakes.note: Never use personal subjects like 'inimesed' (people) with the impersonal form; impersonal verbs exclude an overt subject agent.
The negative impersonal drops the ending '-kse', using 'ei' + impersonal stem (ei räägita).
'Tegema' undergoes stem reduction in the impersonal voice to become 'tehakse'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'Estonian is spoken here' in Estonian?
quiz.explanation: 'Rääkima' becomes 'räägitakse' in the present impersonal.

quiz.question: What is the negative impersonal form of 'sööma' (to eat)?
quiz.explanation: The negative impersonal combines 'ei' with the impersonal stem: 'ei sööda'.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Koolis ___ palju uusi asju.' (õppima)
quiz.explanation: Weak grade stem 'õpi-' takes '-takse', yielding 'õpitakse'.

quiz.question: Which form means 'coffee is drunk' (jooma)?
quiz.explanation: 'Jooma' shifts vowels in the impersonal present to form 'juuakse'.

tip: Notice that when making negative impersonal statements, drop the final '-kse': 'tehakse' becomes 'ei tehta', 'kirjutatakse' becomes 'ei kirjutata'.

title: Semantic Cases (-ni, -na, -ta, -ga)
subtitle: Expressing limit, role, absence, and accompaniment without prepositions
keyPoint: The last four Estonian cases (Terminative -ni, Essive -na, Abessive -ta, Comitative -ga) attach their unchanging suffixes directly to the genitive singular or genitive plural stem.

examples.en: Jalutasime mere äärde ja seisime seal hommikuni.
Noore tudengina reisis ta palju ringi.
Peeter läks kinno oma uue sõbraga.

mistakes.note: The preposition 'koos' requires the comitative case (-ga), never the nominative base form.
The time expression must be in the genitive before attaching the terminative suffix: kella viieni.
The preposition 'ilma' takes the abessive case suffix '-ta' on the noun.

quiz.question: How do you express 'until tomorrow' (homeni vs homseni from 'homme' / 'homse')?
quiz.explanation: Add the terminative -ni to the genitive stem 'homse', giving 'homseni'.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Mari töötab haiglas ___ (arst).' (as a doctor)
quiz.explanation: The essive case suffix '-na' expresses functioning in a role or state ('as an X').

quiz.question: Complete the phrase: 'Tulin linna ___ (rong).' (by train)
quiz.explanation: Means of transport and instruments take the comitative suffix '-ga' ('rongiga').

quiz.question: Choose the abessive form of 'raha' (money):
quiz.explanation: The abessive ending '-ta' signifies 'without' ('rahata' = without money).

tip: Unlike the grammatical and interior cases, these four semantic cases never cause internal stem consonant gradation changes of their own—they just latch straight onto the existing genitive form!

title: Compound Past Tenses (Täisminevik and Enneminevik)
subtitle: Connecting past actions to present or previous timeframes using 'olema' and '-nud'
keyPoint: Compound past tenses combine a conjugated present or past form of 'olema' with the past active participle in '-nud' (or passive '-tud').

useCases.label: Life Experience (Present Perfect)
useCases.example: Kas sa oled kunagi Eestis käinud?

useCases.label: Prior Past Event (Past Perfect)
useCases.example: Kui rong saabus, oli ta juba lahkunud.

examples.en: Ma olen seda raamatut juba lugenud.
Kas te olete juba lõunat söönud?
Eile õhtuks oli ta oma töö lõpetanud.
Me ei ole veel seda uut filmi näinud.
examples.highlight: ei ole veel seda uut filmi näinud

examples.en: Politsei tuli, kui varas oli juba põgenenud.

mistakes.note: The auxiliary verb 'olema' must be paired with the past participle (-nud), never a finite past tense form.
In negative compound tenses, 'olema' uses the invariant negative present auxiliary 'ole' regardless of the plural person.
The past active participle ending is always '-nud', not just '-n'.

quiz.question: How do you form the present perfect 'We have lived here for five years'?
options: Me oleme siin viis aastat elanud.
Me olime siin viis aastat elanud.
quiz.explanation: 'Me oleme ... elanud' uses the present tense of 'olema' (oleme) plus the -nud participle.

quiz.question: Choose the past perfect (enneminevik): 'Before dinner, he ___ (finish) the homework.'
quiz.explanation: The past perfect requires the past form of 'olema' ('oli') plus the past participle ('lõpetanud').

quiz.question: Complete the negative present perfect: 'Nemad ___ veel otsustanud.' (have not)
quiz.explanation: The negative present auxiliary is 'ei ole' (or 'pole').

quiz.question: What is the past active participle of 'kirjutama'?
quiz.explanation: Active past participles form by replacing the '-ma' infinitive marker with '-nud': 'kirjutanud'.

tip: In conversational Estonian, 'ei ole' is very frequently contracted to 'pole' (e.g., 'Ma pole teinud' instead of 'Ma ei ole teinud'). Both are fully correct.

title: Conditional Mood (Tingiv Kõneviis)
subtitle: Expressing hypothetical situations and polite requests with the -ks marker
keyPoint: The conditional mood is formed by adding -ks (plus personal endings if desired) to the vowel stem of a verb, conveying hypothetical conditions, dreams, or polite requests.

useCases.label: Polite Inquiries & Requests
useCases.example: Kas ma saaksin ühe kohvi, palun?

useCases.label: Hypothetical Scenarios
useCases.example: Kui mul oleks aega, reisiksin rohkem.

useCases.label: Past Unreal Wishes
useCases.example: Me oleksime tulnud, kui oleksime teadnud.

examples.en: Kui mul oleks palju raha, ostaksin suure maja.
Kas sa aitaksid mind selle ülesandega?
Ta ei teeks seda mitte mingil juhul.
Kui ilm oleks soojem, läheksime randa.

mistakes.wrong: Kui mul on aega, ma tuleksin.
mistakes.right: Kui mul oleks aega, ma tuleksin.
mistakes.note: In unreal conditional sentences, both clauses must use the conditional mood (-ks), not indicative ('on').
Ensure personal suffixes match: '-ksin' for 'mina' (1st sg) and '-ksite' for 'teie' (2nd pl).
Past conditional requires 'oleks' alongside the past active participle ending in '-nud'.

quiz.question: How do you politely ask 'Could I get water?'
quiz.explanation: 'Saaksin' uses the conditional marker -ks with 1st person ending -in for a polite request.

quiz.question: Complete the hypothetical clause: 'Kui meil ___ aega, me jalutaksime pargis.'
quiz.explanation: The 'if' clause of a hypothetical condition requires conditional 'oleks'.

quiz.question: What is the past conditional of 'nad tulevad' (they would have come)?
quiz.explanation: The past conditional is formed by combining 'oleksid' with the -nud participle 'tulnud'.

quiz.question: Which form is the negative conditional 'I would not say'?
quiz.explanation: The negative marker 'ei' plus the -ks conditional form makes 'ei ütleks'.

tip: In everyday spoken Estonian, speakers often omit the personal ending and use the plain '-ks' across all persons (e.g., 'ma teeks', 'sa teeks', 'me teeks'). You will be understood everywhere!

title: Existential Clauses with Partitive Subjects
subtitle: Expressing presence, availability, and negation with partitive subjects
keyPoint: In existential sentences indicating location or availability, an indefinite or uncountable subject takes the partitive case, and in negative existential sentences, the subject is always partitive.

cells: There is (some) bread on the table.
There are people walking in the park.
There is no milk in the fridge.
The milk is in the fridge.

examples.en: Meil ei ole täna vaba aega.

mistakes.note: Negative existential clauses always require the subject to be in the partitive case (piima), never nominative (piim).
When expressing indefinite existence of plural entities ('there are dogs outside'), use the plural partitive instead of nominative plural.
If you want to say 'there is water in the bottle', start with the location and put the indefinite substance in partitive.

quiz.question: Complete the existential clause: 'Klassiruumis ei ole ___.' (teacher)
quiz.explanation: In negative existential sentences, the subject must be in the partitive case ('õpetajat').

quiz.question: Complete the sentence to show indefinite existence: 'Kaussis on magusat ___.' (apple)
quiz.explanation: Indefinite uncountable or partial quantities in existential clauses take the partitive singular ('õuna').

quiz.question: Which sentence means 'There are children on the street'?
quiz.explanation: Existential word order puts location first ('Tänaval on') followed by partitive plural for indefinite entities ('lapsi').

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Täna ei ole meil mingit ___.' (problem)
quiz.explanation: Negation of existence requires partitive case ('probleemi').

tip: Check word order: if the location comes first (e.g., 'Toas on...'), the following subject is almost always partitive if indefinite or negative!

title: Inflected Forms of the -ma Infinitive
subtitle: Expressing ongoing actions, origins, and absences with -mas, -mast, and -mata
keyPoint: Case endings attach directly to the -ma stem: -mas marks continuous presence at an action, -mast indicates returning from it, and -mata expresses 'without doing'.

cells: He is shopping at the store.
I came here in order to learn Estonian.

examples.en: Ema tuli just turult toitu ostmast.
Vanaisa käib igal hommikul pargis jalutamas.

mistakes.note: To say 'without doing', use the -mata form alone instead of translating 'ilma' with the nominative infinitive.
To indicate being engaged in an action right now, use 'olema + -mas', never the -da infinitive.
Coming from an activity requires the elative case form -mast, whereas -ma expresses destination.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form: 'Marten on köögis lõunasööki ___.' (cooking)
quiz.explanation: 'Olema + -mas' denotes an ongoing physical activity at a location ('is cooking').

quiz.question: Choose the correct form: 'Nad tulid just järve äärest ___.' (swimming)
quiz.explanation: The elative form -mast expresses returning from an activity.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form: 'Ta vastas küsimusele hetkegi ___.' (without hesitating)
quiz.explanation: The abessive form -mata expresses 'without doing'.

quiz.question: Which verb form completes: 'Kirjutasin kirja valmis vigadeta ja pikalt ___.' (without thinking)?
quiz.explanation: '-mata' denotes absence of the action ('without thinking').

tip: Think of the -ma infinitive as a noun stem: just like maja -> majas (in the house) -> majast (from the house), sööma -> söömas (eating) -> söömast (from eating)!

title: Imperative and Jussive Moods
subtitle: Direct commands, prohibitions, and third-person wishes with -ge and -gu
keyPoint: The 2nd person singular imperative uses the bare present stem, while plural commands use -ge/-ke and indirect commands for 3rd person (jussive) use -gu/-ku.

examples.en: Mine kohe koju ja puhka välja!
Ärge unustage oma dokumente kaasa võtta!
Ärgu keegi arvaku, et see on lihtne.

mistakes.note: Prohibitions do not use 'mitte'; use the negative imperative auxiliary 'ära' for singular and 'ärge' for plural.
'Ärge' must be followed by the verb in the -ge/-ke imperative form, never the -da infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: Ta peab tegema seda, las ta teeb!
mistakes.right: Las ta teeb / Ta tehku seda!
mistakes.note: For formal indirect third-person command, use jussive '-gu/-ku' (tehku) or 'las' with present tense, not just a plain assertion.

quiz.question: Choose the correct negative command for 'teie': 'Palun ___ siin suitsetage!'
quiz.explanation: 'Ärge' is the negative command auxiliary for the 2nd person plural ('teie').

quiz.question: Which verb correctly completes the jussive command: 'Igaüks ___ oma vastuse ise.' (should write)
quiz.explanation: The 3rd person indirect command (jussive) uses suffix -gu/-ku ('kirjutagu').

quiz.question: Form the 1st person plural hortative: '___ koos lahendus!' (Let's find)
quiz.explanation: The polite cohortative 'let us do' takes the -kem/-gem ending ('Leidkem').

quiz.question: How do you say to one person 'Don't go yet!'?
quiz.explanation: Single person negative command uses 'ära' + stem ('Ära mine!').

tip: Notice the consonant harmony: strong grade uses -ke/-ku (haka-ke, vaa-daku) while vowels or voiced consonants use -ge/-gu (tul-ge, ol-gu).

title: Quotative Mood (Kaudne Kõneviis)
subtitle: Reporting hearsay and unverified claims using the -vat marker
keyPoint: The quotative mood replaces indicative endings with the invariant suffix -vat (present) or 'olevat' + past participle (past) to signal reported speech or hearsay without committing to its truth.

cells: The Prime Minister has reportedly resigned.
They say he does not know Estonian.
Supposedly the train had not reached the station.

useCases.label: Media and news reporting
useCases.example: Uus teelõik avatavat juba järgmisel nädalal.

useCases.label: Everyday gossip and rumors
useCases.example: Naabrid ostvat uue ja kalli auto.

useCases.label: Distancing oneself from a claim
useCases.example: Ta olevat haige ja ei tulevat koosolekule.

examples.en: Kuulsin, et Jüri elavat nüüd hoopis Tartus.
See film olevat selle aasta parim.
Nad ei teadvat tegelikult asjast mitte midagi.
Röövel olevat põgenenud üle piiri välismaale.

mistakes.wrong: Nad räägivad, et ta on rikas.
mistakes.note: While 'Nad räägivad, et...' is correct grammatically, Estonian stylistically prefers the concise quotative mood 'olevat rikas' in formal and written contexts.
The suffix -vat is added directly to the -da infinitive stem without hyphens or person agreement (it never conjugates for mina, sina, etc.).

mistakes.wrong: Me kuulsime, et nemad elavad seal.
mistakes.note: Using the indicative 'elavad' asserts personal witness or objective truth; use 'elavat' to clearly demarcate hearsay.

quiz.question: How do you express 'Supposedly he is going to Spain' using the quotative mood?
quiz.explanation: The present quotative attaches -vat to the -da stem ('sõita' -> 'sõitvat').

quiz.question: Fill the blank for reported past action: 'Direktor ___ juba lepingu alla kirjutanud.'
quiz.explanation: The past quotative compound tense is formed with the quotative auxiliary 'olevat' + past participle.

quiz.question: What does the invariant suffix '-vat' indicate in Estonian?
options: A condition dependent on an event
quiz.explanation: The quotative mood (-vat) expresses hearsay, rumour, or unverified indirect report.

quiz.question: Choose the correct negative quotative: 'Kuulujuttude järgi ta ei ___ tõtt.' (is not speaking)
quiz.explanation: The negative quotative combines 'ei' with the -vat form: 'ei räägivat'.

tip: The quotative suffix -vat never changes for grammatical person. Mina tulevat, sina tulevat, nemad tulevat — one invariant ending for all!

title: Participles in Clause Shortening
subtitle: Compressing relative and temporal clauses with -v, -tav, -nud, and -tud
keyPoint: Subordinate clauses starting with 'kes', 'mis', or 'kui' can be converted into pre-modifying participial phrases where active or passive participles decline in case and number with their head noun.

useCases.label: Adverbial modifier of result/manner
useCases.example: Ta vastas naeratades ja käsi laiutades.

examples.en: Kodu poole kõndiv noormees kuulas taskuhäälingut.

mistakes.note: When shortened into an adjective-like modifier, the participle ('jooksvat') must agree in case and number with the head noun ('meest' - partitive singular).
The active subject who performed the writing requires the active past participle '-nud' (kirjutanud), not the passive '-tud'.

mistakes.wrong: Auto mis pargitud siin on minu oma.
mistakes.right: Siia pargitud auto on minu oma.
mistakes.note: Participle constructions precede the noun they modify, unlike English and standard relative clauses.

quiz.question: Shorten the clause: 'naine, kes töötab haiglas' -> 'haiglas ___ naine'
quiz.explanation: Active present relative clause ('kes töötab') is shortened using the -v participle ('töötav').

quiz.question: Select the correct form to agree with the noun: 'Andsin võtme laua taga ___ mehele.' (sitting)
quiz.explanation: Participles modifying a noun must agree in case and number: 'mehele' is allative singular, so 'istuvale' must also be allative singular.

quiz.question: Shorten the passive past clause: 'küsimused, mis arutati koosolekul' -> 'koosolekul ___ küsimused'
quiz.explanation: Passive past actions ('mis arutati') shorten to the -tud participle ('arutatud').

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses clause shortening for 'The child who woke up early was tired'?
options: Laps kes vara ärganud oli väsinud.
quiz.explanation: 'Ärkama' is active intransitive in the past, so the correct active past participle is 'ärganud'.

tip: Remember agreement: unlike verbs in finite clauses, the -v and -tav participles decline through all 14 Estonian cases just like regular adjectives to match their head noun!
